sections.text: Hello and welcome to the Skeptics' Guide to the Universe. Today is Wednesday, February 21st, 2024, and this is your host, Steven Novella. Joining me this week are Bob Novella...
Hey, everybody!
Cara Santa Maria...
Howdy.
Jay Novella...
Hey guys.
...and Evan Bernstein.
Good evening folks.
How's everyone doing this fine day?
Doing good.
Doing all right.
Not too shabby.
All right then.
Did the rain finally stop?
Yeah, we're finally in the middle of an actual winter with cold weather and snow and everything.
Really?
Yeah.
Fifteen degrees Fahrenheit this morning.
Ooh, yikes. We had like three days of nonstop rain after we already had those two intense storms. So more mudslides, more flooding.
I heard a lake formed in Death Valley.
I heard that too.
That's how much rain.
What?
Yeah.
And it's gone already.
Outstanding water for several days. Yes.

But it's crazy how like powerful the sun is here. I went outside this morning and everything was still really wet and I just let my dog out before recording and it's like almost bone dry outside already.

So last, two episodes ago, we were chatting about the eclipse coming up in April. And I wanted to clarify a few things that we said during the discussion. So Evan, you said that the old eclipse glasses or solar glasses may not work, right? That they may expire after a certain amount of time.
Yeah. The cheapo ones.

So we were questioned about that. So we looked it up to get all the details. And it turns out that what you're saying is true, but it's a little outdated in that in 2015, there was a requirement in the US at least to adhere to international standards in terms of making solar glasses or eclipse glasses. And those do not automatically expire, right? So you could use them theoretically forever. However, there's a big caveat to that. And a lot of sites point this out, is that that assumes they're in good condition, right? So if you packed them away and put them away somewhere safe, yes, you can take them out again four years later or whatever and they're still good. But if you threw them in a drawer somewhere and they're like scratched or damaged in any way, do not use them. So old glasses comes with a lot of caveats. It's only if you've kept them in good condition. Because even a little scratch, that could be-
A pinhole could do damage.
Yeah. It could do significant damage.
Oh, wow. I mean, they're cheap. Just get new ones at this point.
Yeah. Why risk it? Just get new ones.
Better safe than sorry.
And you'll also know if you go outside and put them on and look up, you'll see. That's the thing about eclipse. They're so obvious.
Oh, yeah.

The sky will be black if you're wearing eclipse glasses in the middle of the day. And the only way that you'll be able to see the sun is if you know where it is and you look straight at it in the glasses.
Anything other than looking directly at the sun is pure blackness.
Yeah.

Right. The other thing is we were talking about when you should use the eclipse glasses and we just made a couple of general comments. But there's a lot of details there too that I was finding out. So one is that, well, of course, I don't think this needs to be said, but we're going to say it anyway. You can never, ever look directly at the sun at any time, at any part of the eclipse. The only time is during total totality. That's the only time you can look directly at the sun is during totality. However, there's one nuance to that that's interesting. At the beginning and at the end of totality, there's the so-called diamond ring effect, right? Where you get a bright rim around the sun.
Almost like a little lens flare.

Yeah. And it lasts for one to two seconds. So the question is, is it safe to look at that without your solar eclipse glasses on? And like when you say, so here I've read multiple recommendations, but most of the like official recommendations from NASA or astronomy or whatever, they say you have the eclipse glasses on when the diamond ring thing happens. When that is done, then you can take the eclipse glasses off. And then at the end of the eclipse, as soon as you see the diamond ring effect, you have to put your solar glasses back on again.

But that part is really, like it takes the amount of time it takes to put glasses on or take them off for that to happen. I think the thing that we have to remember is we're talking about this as if people aren't going to know the difference. It's like, have you ever looked up when the sun was in the sky? Don't look at it. It hurts.
Oh, yeah.
And that's the reason why...

Here's the thing Cara, so this is why there's so much discussion about like, is it safe to look at an eclipse? So you're right. If you look at the sun, it's extremely bright and it's painful. And you know, are your pupils clamped on? You squint, you look away. You can't, you'd have to really try to stare into the sun long enough to burn your retinas. But when enough of the sun is covered, it's the total brightness isn't enough to cause pain or discomfort or to close down your pupils. But that little sliver of light is still bright enough to burn your retina. So that's the most dangerous time is when your protective reflexes aren't in place, but that rim of that crescent of sun is still bright enough to burn your retina. So you're just basically burning up little crescents in your retina while you're looking at the eclipse without that protective effect.

I get that. But I also like, I don't know, in my experience, it's not easy to look at the sun until it's in totality. It's a concerted effort. You are still squinting into the sun if you're trying to look at it with your naked eyes, which you should never do. There's a huge difference between a partial eclipse and a total eclipse. It's massive. And so I more say that not because it's like, of course, I think that that's all really, really good advice. I also think, gosh, I hope people already know not to look at the sun with their naked eyes. I say it mostly because a lot of people are really scared of like, when will I know when it's okay? And it's like, you'll know.
Yeah, you'll know. It's not subtle.

There's a massive difference. It's not something that you have to calculate. It's not something that you have to work out on paper. It's really clear and obvious when you're in partial and when you go into totality.
Right. But don't take the lack of pain during partial eclipses thinking it's okay. I can look at, oh, it's not hurting. I can look at that crescent of sun. No, you can't.
Right. Yeah. Never look at the sun.
Yeah, it will still burn your eyes. It will still burn your retina.
Oh, my gosh. Not a good idea. Nope.

Yeah. And if you want to risk the one or two seconds of watching the diamond ring, that's fine. Just be careful. Just know that it's very quick. And as soon as that crescent appears, you've got to look away and put your glasses back on or whatever. If you blow the timing, as somebody pointed out, it's like if you try to, at the beginning, if you try to take your glasses off before the diamond ring effect so you see it and you get a glare from the crescent sun, that could also spoil your viewing for a while.
It does. Yeah. It bleaches you a little bit. That's true.
Yeah. You're not going to be dark adapted.
Yeah. Just wear your glasses the whole time. You'll know when-
Except in full totality.
Yeah. You'll know when totality happens. It will get dark. The minute it gets dark, you can take them off.
You will see the stars. That's how dark it will get.
Maybe. Depending on where you live. Probably not in LA.
You will see the stars.
Oh, wait. There is no eclipse in LA.
No.
You might not in Dallas proper see the stars. You might.
No. You will. I think you will. Why wouldn't you?
Because of the light pollution.
Well, the lights won't be on.
But will it illuminate during the day? The streetlights, they're not going to turn the streetlights on all of a sudden.

No, but there's a shitload of light pollution all the time. Trust me. If you can't see the stars in a nice clear night in Dallas, you're probably not going to see them in the middle of the day during an eclipse. here's a ton of light pollution.
That's interesting. Yeah.
There's one star I'm going to see, and I'll be looking at it.
Yeah. Well, and you are going to see stars. I mean, I'm just saying it's not going to be like the Milky Way. Don't expect during a total solar eclipse for the sky to suddenly look like Death Valley.
It's not going to be a dark sky viewing event.
Yeah. And also, there's still light all around the horizon. So like you might see a couple stars if you're in a place where it's relatively easy to see stars.
Oh, interesting. Yeah.
But it's not like the sky's-
Saw stars in Oregon. That's for sure.
Yeah. But Oregon is a pretty dark sky. Like there are parts of Oregon that are really dark. I was at least kind of out in the middle of nowhere. Were you also?
Yes. Oh, yeah. Absolutely.
Most people probably won't be for this. Some people will be along the path, but people who are going to like major metropolitan areas for it.
We're in a metropolitan area, I suppose. Yeah. Interesting. I don't know. I've never been in this environment, a metropolitan area during an eclipse. This will be a first.
I hear people cheering and stuff. It's really cool.
Oh, it's going to be amazing. It's going to be so good. Indescribable.
All right, guys. Let's go on with our news items.
Pesticide in Oat Products – Should You Worry? [2]
sections.title: Pesticides in Oats

sections.text: Have you guys heard all the hubbub about the pesticides in like oatmeal and oat products and Cheerios?
Yes.
Oh, I read something about that recently.
I thought I read something about like-
Yeah, terrible chemicals.
-lead or iron, not pesticides. Am I wrong?
The study doesn't bear that out, does it?

So there was a study published by the Environmental Working Group, right? Who is, in my opinion, kind of a... They're an advocacy group, not an objective scientific group. And they tend to always sort of over call the risk of toxicity, you know? So I always like it's... That's a red flag for me if the EWG is involved. So they did a study looking at the levels of a specific pesticide called chlormequat in oat-based products in the United States and in urine samples collected from people in the United States from 2017, 2018 to 2022, and then 2023, those three time periods. Why did they do this? So chlormequat is technically a pesticide because it's an herbicide. And what it does is it reduces the growth of the long stem of certain crops, right? So they don't grow as tall. And that helps in a couple of ways. It reduces the risk that the stalk will bend over or break, and it makes it easier to harvest as well, right? Without affecting, adversely affecting the thing you're trying to harvest, right? The rest of the crop. In the United States presently, it's approved for use in ornamental plants, but not food crops. In the European Union, it's approved for use in food crops like oats. In 2018, the U.S. changed their regulations allowing for the import of grains from the EU that were grown with chlormequat. So we still don't use it in the U.S., but now we are allowing the import of food from the EU that did use it. I was interested in that out of the gate because generally speaking, the EU has stricter regulations and restrictions than the U.S. does. So this was odd that it was flipped. But anyway, so they were measuring, okay, well, is it being found in U.S. food and is it being found in the urine of people in the U.S.? So even before you do the study, the answer is, of course it is because we went from not having it in the food stream to having it in the food stream. So the result seems pretty obvious. But okay, fine. They wanted to see confirm that and see how much. And they found pretty much exactly what they were looking for. Yes, many of the products that they tested, they said all but two of 25 conventional oat-based products had detectable levels of chlormequat in it and with a range of non-detectable to 291 micrograms per kilogram. And they found concentrations in the urine of subjects as well. And that concentration increased from 2018 to 2023 because, of course, it did. And now we're importing oats from Europe that were grown using it. So they basically used this as an opportunity to advocate against the U.S. loosening up the restrictions on chlormequat, which they're considering doing, and saying if you want to avoid it, you can eat organic. You could buy organic stuff, right? So they're shilling for the organic industry and they're always about like more restrictions on anything chemical used in agriculture. So the reporting on this has been horrible because they're basically buying the Environmental Working Groups' framing of this hook, line, and sinker. For example, a headline from a CBS News report, Pesticides Linked to Reproductive Issues Found in Cheerios, Quaker Oats, and Other Oat-Based Food. And then you read the article and it's all just quoting from the Environmental Working Group and without any real context. My first question was, what? What do you guys think? When you hear this story, what's your first question?
There are trace amounts of all kinds of things in our food. How dangerous is the amount of this?
What's the amount? What's the dose?
Yeah. What's the dose.
What did they find?
And what's the outcome of that dose? Like what should we expect from that dose?

Exactly. So there are established safety limits. You know, the U.S. has its safety limit. The European Union has its safety limit. In the U.S., the safety limit is 0.05 milligrams per kilogram body weight per day. And in the European Food Safety Authority, it's 0.4 milligrams per kilogram per body weight per day. So you notice anything about the units so far that I've thrown out there?
Or their kilograms, they're not-
Grams. We're talking metric.
So the amount they're detecting in the oats is in the micrograms per kilogram (µg/kg).
Yeah. That's a millionth of a gram, right?
And the safety limits are in the milligrams per kilogram.
Thousandth of a gram.
So that's three. Yeah. That's three decimals away.

That's three orders of magnitude. And they say in the study that the amounts that we're detecting are several orders of magnitude below the established safety limits. Yeah. Because they are. And, of course, none of the reporting mentions this, right? I actually did a fun calculation. I calculated how many kilograms of oats you would have to eat every day in order to get up to the lower end of the limit of the safety levels the safety regulation.
Can I guess?
Yeah. What do you think?
What measurement are you using?
How many kilograms of oats would you need to eat to get enough chloroquine to exceed the lower limit of the safety levels?
And a kilogram is, what, 2.2 pounds?
Yeah.
Okay.
A centillion tons.
I'd say 10 pounds a day.
Ten pounds a day.
Ten pounds. That's about, what, four kilos?
Four kilos a day.
4.3 kilos.
And you said this is for – you calculated it for what, like rolled oats? Did you also calculate it for something like oatmeal? Is it somehow concentrated?
I used the highest level that they reported.
No, I know what I'm saying in terms – I mean the delivery method because some people drink oat milk. I don't know if it's like – is the concentration higher or lower in something like –
Well, let's say dry oats because I'm just giving you the levels that they detected like in Cheerios or in Quaker Oats or whatever.
All right. So you're saying how many like – how many oats, like actual like bowls of oatmeal?
Yeah. In kilograms.
But in kilograms.
In kilograms.
2.2 pounds.
Because that's what they needed.
It's at least one kilogram. Let's say 12 kilograms. 12 kilos.
Yeah. 10 or 12. I don't know.
85,000 kilograms.
Oh my gosh. It's even worse.
OK. So it doesn't matter.
All your questions are –
We're in homeopathy territory for all intents and purposes.
Exactly.
Yeah.
We're at homeopathic doses of chlormequat.
Yeah, right. Avogadro here.
Now, here's the thing.
You have to eat that every day?
Every day. In the study –
Every day.
In the study –
For what, like three months, right?

They say – no, it's every day. They say, now, we know that these urine levels that we're detecting probably represent ongoing exposure because chloroquine is rapidly eliminated from the body through the urine.
There you go. Kidneys. Thank you.

So this isn't something that built up over time. They must be consuming this every day. It's like, yeah. It's rapidly eliminated from your body through the kidneys. Think about that. That also means that you would have to eat those 85,000 kilograms of oats every single day. Right? And the moment you stop doing that, your body would clear it out of your system. I mean, it's just –
It brings it into the implausibility category.
That's the several orders. So again, it's several orders of magnitude.
Impossible.
Yeah, I'd say impossible.

It's impossible. Obviously, it's impossible. But not only that, but when the EU and the EPA, whatever, when they establish safety limits, they're already going one or two orders of magnitude below the lowest dose that was shown to cause toxicity. Right?
Always?

Yeah. They take like – Yeah. They use the data, usually animal data. So at this dose, we start to see adverse health effects. So let's go one or two orders of magnitude below that, and that's where we'll set our safety limit. That's standard procedure. So then you go three orders of magnitude further below that.
I always wondered about the politics of that for something like lead back in the day. I would have assumed they would have erred in the other direction, sadly. I'd be wrong.

No, that's the standard procedure. Go at least an order of magnitude below where you start to see adverse effects. So no one mentioned this. Then they say – Also, the toxicity that they're talking about, like the reproductive issues, that's only in animals. Never been shown in humans.
Yeah.
And it's shown in animals at massive doses. Again, at these kinds of ridiculous doses, right? Of course, because that's where you set the – That's how the safety limits were set. So it's ridiculous.
Because you can probably feed a farm animal pounds and pounds of oats, but like we don't do that.
It's still fine. It's 80,000 kilograms, Cara.
That's great.
It's ridiculous. The whole thing is silly. It's silly.
It's like a silo of oats or something, right? I mean how –
Is there an animal that can eat that much?

So what's the – The only thing I could see that the purpose of this whole thing is just to create a round of fear mongering in the press to lobby against the U.S. changing regulations to shill for organic food. When I wrote about it on Science Based Medicine in the comments, someone pointed out, it's also – Another thing, whether this is their purpose or not, it also accomplishes the goal of leveling the playing field between traditional or standard agriculture and organic. Because if you basically deprive agriculture of using all of the science and technology that we have available, then it narrows the benefit that the increased productivity and cost effectiveness and land use and all that, that standard agriculture has above organic agriculture. It's like you can't use GMOs. You can't benefit from GMOs because they're trying to ban it because then that narrows the gap of the advantage over organic, right? So it also creates the – Well, just eat organic just to be safe. You know, because then – Just to be safe.
Be extra safe.
Yeah. It's absolutely ridiculous. This is why I have a massive problem with the Environmental Working Group because they pull this kind of shit all the time.
And the media is, of course, willing to go along on the ride.

Yeah. They didn't want to spend – Whatever. Because this is being reported probably by people who are not science journalists and they're quoting experts, right? So they think their job is done. They didn't take the 10 minutes it would take to ask the most basic question. It's like, well, they just quote somebody from the EPA that's saying this is below safety limits, right? And then they quote somebody from Quaker Road saying we follow all regulations, which always sounds like – Even though it's true.
Yeah, it sounds sketchy as hell.
It sounds sketchy as hell because – Yeah, because –
We follow all regulations.
It's designed to meet legal scrutinies, right? Anything that can be used against them in court.
It sounds like boilerplate denial, right? And rather than saying-
Yeah, boiler speak.

Yeah, we asked an independent scientist to tell us what's going on here and put it into some context for it, and they told us you'd have to eat 80,000 kilograms every day for this to be of any concern. Whatever.
Right. Which we don't recommend doing anyway.
– Which we don't recommend. Yeah, right. By the way, people-
Kill you. For other reasons.
You would die of a million other things before you died of this toxicity if you consumed that much.
The chlormequat would be the least of your problems, yeah.
I think you would explode, like, all of your organs.
I'm getting gassy just talking about this.
Sora is an AI model that can create realistic and imaginative scenes from text instructions. [3]
sections.title: AI Video

sections.text: All right, Jay, tell us about the AI and video. We've been talking about this.
Oh, boy.

So you guys have heard of OpenAI, right? Everybody has. Well, they recently introduced the next digital demon called Sora. It's pretty Bob, AI it's good and scary at the same time. So the product is called Sora, S-O-R-A, and this is a sophisticated artificial intelligence system that is designed to convert text, similar to, like, DALL-E or MidJourney. It converts text into photorealistic video, not an image, a video, a 60-second video. This is a massive milestone, and it's another leap in AI technology, and it's a huge step forward for OpenAI's technology suite. Other companies have text-to-video, and many others are working on it, but Sora looks to be way ahead of the rest of them. I was doing some research. There really isn't anything to see from any other companies. There's a lot of chatter about this company's working on this, this company's working on that, but this seems to be the first one to make it to market that has a photorealistic quality. So, of course, there's a mix of excitement for the potential to enhance the creative space, and we can produce educational content there's lots of ways it could be used, but there are also a huge list of legitimate concerns over the implications for misinformation, disinformation, and particularly during this critical election period that's going to be happening over the next year. So, Sora is unique in that it can generate videos, like I said, up to 60 seconds in length from simple text instructions or a combination of text and images. I know you guys were talking about this on the live stream last Friday. Cara, I don't know if you have, but I could send you a link just so you could take a look at what types of video that this can produce. It's remarkable.
Remarkable.

The videos that I saw, remarkable. One of the best ones I saw was a woman walking down a city street that looks like a neon-lit Tokyo. Just, I would have no reason to think it wasn't real. There was just not one indication in there to my eyes that it wasn't real. The human faces, the movement, excellent. Like one detail I saw where there was somebody that was carrying a shopping bag, and it was kind of like bouncing off their leg and moving erratically like a shopping bag would if you're hitting it with your leg as you're walking, like that level of quality. So, of course, we really won't know the ins and outs until we can use the product ourselves, but they're showing us, of course, the most impactful videos that they came up with. But there's no reason to think that in a short matter of time they're going to open this up and we're all going to be using it and it's going to be easy to use. I mean, they show you the prompts, the textual prompts.
Yeah, they show you the prompt.

And a typical prompt would be like what I wrote. A woman walking down a city street in Tokyo with lots of neon lights. You know, that's all it would take to generate this 60-second video. There's a major creative problem that I think we should discuss very briefly. Steve and I have the most experience with this. This problem with current image creation software. I've used DALI. I've used MidJourney. And the thing that they can't do well right now is they can't handle specific instructions. Steve and I were just talking about Steve was making an image. He was making for a tabletop game that he was playing and he was trying to get a gem to appear in the middle of a medieval shield. And he just couldn't get the software to do it. And the thing is, it makes you an image and you can't say, take this image that you just made and add a gem in the center of the shield because it'll just generate a brand new shield. It doesn't like follow. So you're kind of starting from scratch every time you go and you just, you modify the text that you're using to kind of get you in the area where you want it to be. But there is no specific instructions here to change minute details. So if Sora has the same limitation, which I guarantee you it will have, its usefulness in the beginning are going to suffer quite a bit because you can't say, have the woman walk a little faster. You probably won't be able to do things like that. And that's if people are going to be using this to make like, movies and stuff, which eventually they will, that functionality I guarantee you just won't be there in the very beginnings of this because again the technology is young. It doesn't get more young than this.
But that seems like an easily fixable problem though.

Yeah. I mean, that's just from a creative standpoint. I thought that would be an interesting thing to throw out there because we have a lot of experience working with AI image generators and like that's a massive flaw that they all have. So now let's get into what I think are the big warning signs here and what I'm worried about and what the experts are actually saying. So this technology will suddenly put us into a world where we just can't trust anything that we see and very soon we can't hear anymore. And once they marry the ability to fake voices, which we could do very well right now, when they marry that to the video footage, people are going to be able to generate pretty much anything that they want and we're not going to know what's real and what's not real. Now they're saying at OpenAI they're taking caution and they have a group called the Red Team that's testing the AI models for safeguards against misuse. This sounds great. This testing phase involves experts and misinformation, hateful content, bias and their goal is to identify and mitigate potential avenues for abuse. That's great and I really am glad that they're doing that. But people will find a way and this is just one company. What if a company comes up with this technology a year from now and they're in another country that doesn't have regulations and that will happen. So it's great that OpenAI is doing this and I just don't see the world getting on the legislation aspect of this so quickly that companies are not going to be able to do the thing that we're all afraid of, which is putting stuff out there and we no longer know what reality is. So here's a list that I gathered from a few different people like Oren Etzioni, who is the founding CEO of the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence. This person has played a significant role in the development of ethical consensus for artificial intelligence technologies. So I borrowed some of his items. I was reading through a lot of different people's list of like these are the potential threats that we're putting up against. So here's the list. Proliferation of deepfakes, right? Sora could significantly enhance the ability to create deepfake videos, making it difficult for the average person to distinguish between what's real and what's not real. That's big. Misinformation and disinformation, right? This tool could be used to generate fake news, misleading content. I mean, I think this is the first thing people are going to do with it, is just use it to make content that's not true, but seemingly real. Security concerns, right? There's high quality video. Deepfakes could be used for malicious purposes like impersonating people, fraud, targeting individuals and institutions. It has threats to creative industries. We've talked about this, but now that people will be able to make video, I would say in a handful of years, people are going to be making movies on these platforms. So that's a big shift. It's going to affect a lot of people with a lot of copyright issues. It's just going to explode. The word explode is not big enough, but it will be an explosion of copyright issues, job losses, a change to culture. Very, very powerful, what this video capability is going to be. It's going to introduce a lot of problems. There's ethical and moral concerns, the ease of creating realistic video content. People are going to be able to make porn and all sorts of stuff like that. It's putting celebrity faces on porn and things like that. It's going to happen.
Unless they build in protections.

Sure. But like I said, Steve, OpenAI will probably not be a company that will let that happen with their stuff. But what about the 30 other companies that are going to be able to do this? So there's going to be regulatory challenges. Like I was saying, right now the framework to do this framework to deal with AI is loose. It's not good. And the government is not moving. U.S. government, I'm talking about, not moving fast enough. And to be quite honest with you, the people that are making decisions don't really grasp this technology. They're not the right people to make the decision. We need professionals who really understand this stuff to help form the regulation. I mean, this list just keeps going on. I have a lot more. I can't even get to all of it here. There's just a lot of reasons why we have to be very, very careful with this. And no matter what, it's going to change our culture. And it's going to change a lot of things. Unpredictable things, as we always say. Like every time we can get an idea of what something can do, there's a hundred things that we can't predict. So that said, I do think that there could be an incredible benefit for creativity. It's going to allow people who don't have the ability to make video, to make lifelike video and a lot of creation can happen. That's all wonderful. And I think if it was limited to that use, there could be a lot of really cool stuff that comes out of it. But the potential here for danger is extraordinary. So I am like, I don't even know if I'm enthusiastic about this. I think it's too early for me to just say, I think this is great. Let's lean into it. I think this is scary and we need to be very cautious. And I think we all have to be prepared for what's going to happen in the next couple of years.

Yeah. I'm excited about it and cautious. I think those two things are not usually exclusive. I mean, I'd love to get my hands on it. And again, I'd love to see where it's going to be in four or five years. sections.text: We are joined now by Chris Smith. Chris, welcome to the Skeptics Guide.

Well thank you very much for having me and what an honour this is. I've listened to your program many times and many colleagues listen to your program. And it's a bit like when Robbie Wiliams said, wanted to be an Oasis, well this is my Robbie Williams wanted to be an Oasis moment. So thank you for having me.

That's very kind. Thank you so much. So Chris, you are from the Naked Scientists podcast, which I've listened to many times, so right right back at you with all of that. But was reading your website in preparation for this and it says that the Naked Scientist podcast was created in 2001.
Yeah, it was.
That was before podcasts existed though. So guess you were just like a recorded radio program at that point?

It was really interesting actually because started making radio programs in 1999 as a mistake. Ended up in a radio studio by mistake. I was a medical student in the middle of my PhD in the middle of my medical degree and after doing that for a year we actually started having appeared on other people's programs making our own science radio show on commercial radio. This is something we just do once a week when we had some free time. And the audience wasn't huge for that commercial radio station. I think we probably got five or six thousand people who would tune in live to that program. But it was on a rock music station. I mean that's not bad for what was ostensibly a local radio broadcast on a rock music station where science was definitely not normally part of the station vocabulary. But it occurred to me that with the internet becoming sufficiently robust by then, it was the year 2000. We probably could get away with putting reasonable sized files, audio files, online and then just giving them away for people to download because at that time it was beginning to become a thing that you try and put your radio show or whatever on the internet as well but people were using real audio. Do you remember those days of real player or as one friend dubbed it real virus because he is to install all this other overhead and all this baggage on your computer and basically hijack your computer. And we thought well why are we tethering people to their desktop when actually probably people would quite like to listen to us on the go. So we just created a way that people could grab the program as an MP3 compressed file and take it away with them and initially just they had to come to the website to do that but there was already this this concept of RSS, really simple syndication. And it wasn't much more to then say well instead of pointing that at just a web page you could actually point that at an audio file so we started doing that. And of course this is what became known as podcasting when iTunes entered the fray and Ben Hammersley pointed that this was something that we could call podcasting in Wired magazine about five years later. So we were already doing that for quite a few years and of course when podcast and then became really quite significant, we were already doing a lot of it and there was one iTunes music store for the world and we were about number three in it and blew up a couple of web servers doing that. But it did get us a lot of prominence, a lot of listeners, some of whom have stayed with us for over 20 years so we're now celebrating our 22nd year of doing this and and some of those people are still there listening. More for them, no I'm only joking.
Yeah just looking up our RSS started in 1999.
Wow.

So that, yeah, that was right then. Yeah, we started in 2005. By then, RSS was already up and running. We also did just put our files on our website, but very quickly, as we grew, went to a media host. And that was also about six months before Apple iTunes started with a podcast category. So we started just before a podcast really were a thing. Here we are, 19 years later. It's been a wild ride.

It's interesting, isn't it? Because remember having a conversation with someone at the BBC and they were busy trying to design formats and ways that would get people tuning into their radio station and said, look, in the future people are going to jump in their car and they won't have an FM radio they won't have an AM radio definitely not. And they definitely won't be deciding which station to tune into. They will basically have an internet connection, and they'll listen to anything they like. They won't be constrained by geography. And I didn't realize really quite how prescient that was at the time. I mean that was just me kind of speculating as a kind of young and enthusiastic kind of tech savvy student. But it's certainly the way it is now and it's come to pass, every car that's being sold now has an internet connection one way or another and is downloading digital audio with that streaming or whether that is pre-made, pre-recorded programs like this one, but that's the way it is.  And so really we've broken the bounds of geography and the constraints of traditional radio, and that's why it's popular, because it is something you take away with you, take on the go, consume on your terms, not when a broadcaster decides that that actually is what you should be listening to right now. And that empowerment is what makes it very very attractive to people because it caters for all tastes.
Yeah, absolutely.
Yeah I can't remember the last time just listened to like radio.

Well tried and it didn't go well. I mean not only a US sale by adverts every 10 seconds but it's more that it just becomes frustrating because you think well l'm not really in the mood for that right now. And someone else's choice of what you want they don't know you because they're not you and so they're trying to second-guess what will appeal to you. Now some news programs do that really well. And there's still a place for I think live broadcasting bringing you up to the moment here and now type material. And news is certainly one part of that. But the rest of the time I don't think it's quite so easy to justify anymore the spend that broadcasters put into radio. And I think digital materials that people can binge on, because that's the nature of the behavior, isn't it? People tend to sort of binge and purge as it were. They grab a whole lot of content listen to it and then delete it all and fill their machine up with something else.

Yeah, I recently had a, like a free month of XM, and I got to say that that XN was actually pretty good because it's clean as hell is like no static, very very clear. And if was in the mood for like oh, I just want to hear some comedy, I would throw that on. And that was actually good or if I wanted to say oh, I'll listen to the Beatles and that was good. But once that month was up you like yeah, I don't want to spend $15 a month you get another monthly fee and just went back to my audio books as usual on my phone. But it was a nice diversion but it's still not as good as just listening to what want to listen to what what book I'm listening to right now is more important than that stuff.

The only downside of course is that the ability to be introduced to new stuff is a little bit diminished. Whereas you end up with this sort of AI system deciding and it's the same with music. This is the kind of music that Chris likes to listen to so serve I'll him up more of the same. So you do need a little bit of unpredictability. They need to program into the algorithm a little bit of curveballism. To make sure, yeah, to make sure you do get exposed to something because otherwise there is a real danger we all fall into a particular groove that we don't then step outside of. And think that that would be a shame. And one of the great benefits of the way we used to do radio is that you would be confronted with guests. You would be confronted with stories or other viewpoints that you otherwise, perhaps, that will challenge you, that you otherwise might not have sought out or been willing to consider and it does help you to engage with those different viewpoints and perspectives. And there is a danger if you self-select is a bit like Twitter just as we used to call it going and finding you loads of people who agree with you rather than finding you people who don't, want to cancel you. And so I think there is there is something to be said for that.

Yeah, I agree. I think that's a big problem where basically our content is increasingly being fed to us by algorithms who care only for the amount of money that we're ultimately feeding into the system, not for our well-being, not for our ability to discover new things or interface with people who disagree with us. Yeah, they want to cocoon us and radicalize us and keep us focused on one thing.
Yeah.
Over and over again.

Remember, Steve, I think we were talking on the show once about how YouTube, if you follow the algorithms, certain algorithms on YouTube, it leads you down a very nasty, dangerous rabbit hole of increasing, extremism in the videos that they want you to watch.

I just watch videos about how to repair land rovers, which is my present project. So actually don't end up down too many rabbit holes, but just people who do geeky things like me so I'm pretty safe I think.
So Chris, you are as you said, you went to medical school, you are a medical doctor by training. You're a microbiologist, correct?

Yes, so what we do with our training in the UK is dual accredit in microbiology, which gives you medical microbiology and virology. So as a virologist I can go and flirt with bacteria as well. But my real focus is viruses and, so you can imagine with what the world has just been through. That was also a pretty hectic ride because how many virologists are there that make radio programs. I mean we have a program on the BBC or National Radio on the BBC, a program on National Radio in Australia. So you can imagine that was quite busy over the last few years as well as doing our own stuff. I would basically go to the lab, do day job, come home and then sit there and do about did did 3,000 interviews over the pandemic for pretty much every network in the world as far as can make out. But it was great for brand awareness. I mean I was at the point where people would actually come and say hello in the street because this was television as well. So I had my sort of moment of stardom and luckily that sort of faded now because I was getting stopped in supermarkets and people would start asking me for travel advice and things like that. And it was getting a little bit frustrating but no it was it was lovely actually that people seem to really be grateful for that effort that we went to to try to make the information clear for everybody.
Well Chris just waited five years. You're going to be just hankering for the next pandemic. You're going to be just like, come on, bring it.

Well, you know what they say? Never waste a good crisis. And other people often say in the same way that we're running out of anti-malarials now and people say well we need another war. We could end up getting that couldn't we? But we need a war in the tropics because inevitably in rush is a huge investment into particular sectors when there is a crisis. And COVID has done wonders for mRNA vaccination, it's done wonders for people's understanding, appreciation, and I think support for medicine, viruses, virology, emerging infections and the mechanisms that cause all those to happen. So I think it's translated into a huge amount of public understanding. So in that respect, it's been valuable, but obviously at a high price.

Yeah, obviously nobody would want a pandemic like that, but it was good for media, not just for science media. But you, on the Naked Scientists, you covered lot of different areas of science. So you're actually a science journalist as well as a medical specialist.

Yes, I took a year off from medicine when I was first a junior doctor, having done a degree, a medical degree and a PhD and then a couple of years of acute general medicine said I'm going to pause for a bit and do something a little bit different. And got a Winston Churchill Memorial Trust Fellowship that enabled me because they fund if you go to them with ideas they will support or did support ideas that are judged to be a once in a lifetime opportunity. And I'd met up with a guy who basically taught me a lot of what know about making science radio who was at the ABC in Australia and he said we'll fix it for you to to work with us for six months to a year. Come and join us in Sydney at the ABC and all you've got to do is worry about how you're going to get funded and that's why I got this funding from the Winston Churchill Memorial Trust, because said, look, I have the opportunity of a lifetime. I've started this thing. It's a small scale radio program and internet radio show which is what we were calling it in those days and I said the thing is I've never had any proper formal training in how to be a journalist. I'm getting tens of thousands of downloads from people all around the world. I think this is going to be quite significant, but I really think out of a sense of responsibility, I need to make sure I'm doing this right. A, not to waste the opportunity, but B, to make sure I'm doing justice to science as well and got interviewed by a panel of great for this fellowship and one of them was Roger Bannister the guy who who ran the mile incredibly quickly, amazing neurologist and couldn't believe was sitting in a room with this guy asking me questions about this, but I made them a pitch and they agreed to fund me. So off I went to Australia and joined the ABC for six months, my wife went as well, she worked doing emergency medicine at Manley Hospital, which doesn't exist anymore, it's a housing estate now, but we had the most amazing time living in Sydney, but while was there, did some research at the university at the same time, but spent most of the week at the ABC each week, and that's where really cut my teeth learning what a story is, how to turn a story which is in a journal into they'll give you two or three minutes of national radio airtime on the breakfast show. They'll say, right, you got three minutes and you got to get that story a paper in nature or science, a top tier journal. You got to get that across to a general audience. And it was see to if you pant stuff, but got to learn to do that and do it quite well and they were obviously sufficiently impressed because for the next 15 years I carried on doing that as the science correspondent for ABC Radio National. And that's why we still have that relationship with them today with our program being broadcast there every Friday. And so it's a lovely connection across the planet. Programs that start life at Cambridge University where I'm based and then are broadcast in various places all over the world. Also in South Africa, we have a couple of programs in South Africa, those are phonin type programs, and on National Radio on the BBC, and half of the airtime, they're hour-long programs, but half of the airtime because we sit in a news slot on the BBC, so we devote half of the program to cutting-edge science news and then the other half of the airtime each week we devote to a topic which usually is pegged to something in the news but we've got a little bit more time to develop the story over that half an hour. So it's both a mixture of fast-paced news with some documentary style production.

How do you feel the gig of science communication has changed over the last 20 years, with social media and the internet and the pandemic and everything. Do you feel like you're getting a lot more pushback from the public or? How would you characterize your career over that time?

Well I think it was quite a young discipline, it still is a young discipline when I started doing this. But it was something that was beginning to gain momentum. And the way got started is that when I was doing my PhD a friend of mine who actually started the naked scientist with, she was funded by one of our research councils and she had in her pigeonhole one day this piece of paper and it said "new grant scheme for the new millennium" And it was an opportunity to bid for some money to get little projects off the ground for early career scientists. And so we filled this thing in and as students we ended up with this actually quite substantial grant actually to do science communication so it was beginning to get going around the year 2000 in a way where people realize that this isn't something that just people who are writing for newspapers or whatever. And their real training was to be a news journalist and they do a bit of science. There was this whole idea about having a specialist who would do science communication but also getting but also getting someone who was a specialist scientist involved, going to the horse's mouth as it were. And think it has grown from there, but I think there's equally a lot of respect for the fact that to do it really well you've got to do it almost whole time or give a substantial amount of your time. It's not something that you mainly do something else and occasionally do a little bit of science journalism. I think to be one of those really, really good people, those people who are really, really, really good writers, really, really very good journalists, they are devoting themselves to this whole time. They're not sort of flirting with it and it took me a long time to sort of regard myself as a journalist. I used to think of myself as a scientist and a doctor who did a bit of science communication and now do feel a little bit more that can say am a journalist because I think have demonstrated that can do that and do that quite well. So feel justified but for a long time felt quite uncomfortable on encroaching on other people's turf and calling myself a journalist because felt I was a little bit of a phoney journalist. I do now think I've demonstrated that I can do this quite well. And think people are actually quite grateful that there are people who are specialists who know about their topic who are also willing to go out there and get in front of a camera or get behind a microphone and bring their topic into the living rooms, the cars, between the years of people who that's not their specialism, but you've got someone who you feel you can trust to do justice to the subject and to you and bring the two things together.

Yeah, it really does require dual expertise, you need expertise in science and in journalism, science communication. And I think for you do as well. You know a lot of scientists who are great scientists, but really any kind of public communication is an afterthought and they don't realize that they don't know how to do it. At the same time know a lot of journalists who do science news who just aren't, they just they're not scientists and it shows. So it's really tricky to bring all of those various completely different skill sets together. There's not really that many people who I think do that exceptionally well.

I think I'm a much better doctor because I went down this path, because it made me much better as a communicator with patients. And also doing this sort of thing as a doctor you understand what the general public tend to understand better. So you don't assume the wrong amount of knowledge or too much knowledge and then bamboozle people. Because got used to the level to pitch medicine at when I'm trying to explain that to patients and then it was a question of would translate that to other topics and realize that there are lots of words that we use as scientists that it's taken us 20 years to become and happy to use them. And they just completely bamboozle people and probably the most important lesson ever learned and think I've thought about this many times. I think what set me on the path when first went to medical school it was my first day at medical school. And I didn't realize we were being set up, but they put us in this lecture theatre. There were 300 medics and dentists in this room. And this lecture started and it was really fierce. It was terrifying. The pace was really high. They were using these words that had no idea what any of this was about and looked around the room and I felt some relief in the sense that I wasn't the only one who clearly had a heart rate of over 150, was sweating profusely. And I was beginning to question whether I'd made a bad career choice. And this went on for 30 minutes, 35 minutes, they would begin to pick on people, puling people out of the audience, humiliating them in front of the rest of the room. And was just about to get up and walk out and think, I think my medical career is over and then this slide went up and it said you have been weaseled, welcome to medical school. And this guy stood up at the front and said now, I want you all to realize that in the next five to six years you're here you're going to learn five to six thousand new words probably. And if you use those words which were a very powerful weapon in front of the patients that you end up treating they're going to end up feeling like you do right now. And think that was one of the most important lessons ever learned in my life which is the power of words and also that what those words will do to people who don't understand them. Because they're not thick, they just haven't had the chance to learn them. I wasn't thick when I sat down that day in that lecture theatre. But I haven't had six years of medical school. And that made a huge impression on me and it never left me as you can probably tell. And I think that really needs passing on to many people because we end up in our laboratories and we talk to each other and we think that unless we use all these long words, complicated language and sound like we swallowed a medical encyclopedia, people will think less of us. But in fact it's the reverse and people think less of us when we're incomprehensible rather than when we make things simple and accessible for everyone to understand.

Yeah I totally agree. That's a great way to put it. So those 5,000 words, I mean you're talking about like everything to do with your career, this is all like professional words that professionals use or- give me more ideas about that.

Well there's two hundred and six bones in the human body and I hadn't heard of any of them really apart from your ass and your elbow when I started. You know anatomy, there's hundreds of different anatomical terms most of it's all in Latin. Then you've got all of the conditions and neoplasia now when we want to talk about cancer in front of a patient but flag it up to another doctor without the person actually realizing you described it as a possible neoplasm, let's see some blood tests and just check because then the person won't twig that you're saying. Well, we better just rule out cancer. So you can use it hopefully under certain circumstances but if you turn around someone and say yes well do you think you've got a neoplasm and they're going to look at you blankly until you say what oh sorry I meant cancer and then of course their world falls apart. So it's really important to make sure you use the right word in the right context. So there are pros and cons to this.

How much do you find that you confront pseudoscience? Because we are a critical thinking science podcast, which is kind of a special sub-nish, I think, of science communication. And the Naked Scientists is more of a straightforward science communication podcast. But how much do you feel like you have to confront the misconceptions and the pseudoscience and the conspiracy theories and not just talk about the science. Or do you feel like you can comfortably ignore that and just present straightforward science?

I think there's a danger. If you go out there saying I'm going to myth bust, that A, people will remember the myth and not the reality, that's always a danger. And B, it comes over as quite confrontational sometimes and it plays into the hands of the people who actually are trying to talk down. A good example of this is the other day I did a program for the BBC on one of our network programs and there was a question about measles.
